question.text: EMA (Exponential Moving Average) differs from SMA (Simple Moving Average) in that:

answer.text: EMA gives more weight to recent prices, making it more responsive to new information
SMA gives more weight to recent prices
EMA and SMA are exactly the same calculation

explanation.text: The Logic: A Simple Moving Average (SMA) treats every price in its lookback window equally — each period gets the same weight when computing the average. An Exponential Moving Average (EMA) applies exponentially decreasing weights, so the most recent prices carry the most influence and older prices fade quickly. That weighting scheme makes EMA more responsive to new information than an SMA over the same window, which is why short-term traders often prefer EMA-based signals. The Trap: EMA does not ignore recent prices — it emphasises them. SMA does not give more weight to recent prices — by definition it weights every observation in the window equally. EMA and SMA are not the same calculation; they share inputs but differ in their weighting formula. Note: The cited NISM Series XV Research Analyst workbook pages checked (pp.295-325, including p.317) discuss moving averages and reference 13/21/34-period EMAs, but do not explicitly define EMA versus SMA or state that EMA weights recent prices more heavily. The explanation above reflects general industry definition of these moving averages.
